Point Sampling in Hardwood Forests at Camp Forest Hills, Springfield IL

By

Alex Chen

Presented to Prof. Jamie Smith

In Partial Fulfillment of the Requirements for
ENV 101
04/21/2025

Introduction
Ensuring accurate forest inventory is essential for creating sustainable forest management. Point sampling, or variable radius plot sampling, is often used to help estimate per-acre and tract values for basal area, tree density, and timber volume, to better understand current and future resources (Lund, 1982). This method employs a Basal Area Factor (BAF) prism in or to select trees that are proportional to their cross-sectional area (Lund, 1982). In point sampling, sample points are used as reference centers for collecting measurements of surrounding trees. These points do not represent the physical area, but instead acts as an anchor for the sampling process by determining which trees are included in a plot based on limiting distances using a prism (Lund, 1982). The use of a BAF prism allows for the inclusion of trees in proportion to the basal area, which can be an efficient method in uneven-aged stands (Lund, 1982). The point sampling method is an important resource for inventory frameworks and can help track possible temporal and spatial changes in forest conditions, and facilitates faster data collection over larger areas (Lund, 1982).
The survey conducted at Camp Forest Hills, Springfield Illinois, used a BAF 10 prism and included all trees above five inch diameter at breast height (DBH). Merchantable volume was recorded for pulpwood (8’ sticks to 4” top diameter) and sawlogs (10” minimum top diameter, measured in ½-log increments). With the data collected from this survey, the results will be compared to a previous survey using the fixed area plot cruise method, using CV%. Strip cruise, fixed area plot, and point sampling will be compared and an analysis of the pros and cons of using individual tally sheets or cumulative tally sheets will be included as well.


Methods
In a field crew of 4, at Camp Forest Hills in Springfield, IL on April 8, 2025, a forest stand was evaluated using the point sampling techniques. The latitude and longitude were 41°50'00"N 87°39'00"W, and the forest stand was mostly comprised of hardwood species such as oaks, maples, and hickories. The equipment comprised of a map of the site, 15 tally sheets, two cruising/Biltmore sticks, two compasses, two logger’s tape, a clipboard, and a Suunto Clinometer.
Plots were established based on the provided map (Figure 1), with a plot point established every 3 chains. 7 plots in total were established and tallied for (Figure 2) At each plot, a BAF 10 prism was used to determine which trees were “in” or “out” of the plot and if they needed to be measured. Trees that were “in” were measured using either a Biltmore stick or logger’s tape. All trees within the plot were measured at DBH using 2” scale D-classes, and trees that were in the 6-inch to 10-inch class or larger trees with a lack of adequate sawlog were evaluated as pulpwood. Trees in the 12-inch class and above were measured as sawlog values to the nearest  ½ log. Each tree was only tallied once. Trees that were considered borderline had their distance from the tree center to the plot center measured, and if it was smaller than the R value found in piR^2, then the tree was considered in.The dot-tally method was used to record the trees in each plot, with one tally sheet per plot. This data was then used to create a stand and stock table (Table 1), with attached equations explaining how these values were calculated (Appendix D).



Discussion
	Within the per-acre estimates, there was a notable concentration of pulpwood and cords within the 14-22 inch classes. Pulpwood had its highest values in the 8 inch class, and sawlog values had its highest values in the class as well. The variability across the DBH class is indicated by their high standard deviations and wide confidence intervals. This variability is common in uneven-aged stands, or in forests going through a transition period due to natural disturbances or management. There was a low amount of trees found in ≥32" DBH classes, which may indicate that these trees may not have had enough time to grow into the upper classes, possibly due to insufficient time since stand initiation. 
	When comparing the coefficient of variation between point sampling and fixed area plot sampling, both had large CV% for pulpwood values per entire tract, with point sampling with a CV% of 155.6% and fixed area plot CV% of 156.07%. These high CV% in both sampling methods indicate variability in the pulpwood volume values between the diameter classes and tally point cheers. This is usually expected in point sampling, since larger trees have a greater influence on estimates since they are more likely to be included within a plot due to being tied to their basal area. Both methods also had high sawlog CV% values as well. This variability is common in point sampling when less larger trees are measured during sampling, and also reflects the sensitivity of using point sampling to measure larger trees with more merchantable volume.
	Point sampling can be beneficial when measuring stands where larger trees make up a large portion of the stand values. However it can also introduce higher variability in uneven-aged stands. Fixed area plots may offer more consistent estimates in more uniform stands, but can sometimes under-represent larger trees unless the plot size is adjusted. Strip cruising can provide clear spatial coverage and is effective at mapping stand variation, but is not as efficient in obstructed terrain and may have biases depending on where the strips are placed. Fixed area plots are useful for stands with more uniform spacing and are compatible with a wide range of forest attributes, but may underrepresent certain trees and there is fixed effort per plot. Point sampling is efficient for sampling basal area and volume, and fewer plots are required, but can be biased in stands with variable size classes and towards larger trees.

Tally sheets are another factor to consider when doing surveys. Individual tally sheets are beneficial for statistical analysis for mean per plot and standard deviation and makes error checking easier to decipher, but requires more data management and can sometimes lead to transcription errors. Cumulative tally sheets can streamline data collection and reduce the risk of plot mislabeling, but can make it difficult to calculate CV% and confidence intervals and loses variance estimation.

Conclusion
	Point sampling can be an effective method for collecting data such as basal area, tree density, and timber volume, and can be less labor intensive and have faster data collection in comparison to methods such as strip cruises and fixed area plots. Point sampling can be effective for uneven-aged stands, but does come with the bias of over-representing larger trees due to their tendency to be included in the view of the BAF prism. When choosing a method to use in the field, it is important to observe the site and the time limit you have to complete a survey. It is also important to consider how you will record your data, as cumulative tally sheets and individual sheets come with positives and negatives depending on what you want to accomplish in the field or when analyzing data afterwards.


Influence of Coloration on Behavioral Interactions and Spatial Preferences in Amphiprion ocellaris Clownfish

Jordan Lee, Morgan Davis, Taylor White, Alex Chen

State University

Department of Environmental Sciences

ENV 202 Monday Section

12/04/2024

Abstract
The False Percula Clownfish (Amphiprion ocellaris) displays color morphs ranging from orange-red to black, raising questions about the role of coloration in behavior. This study investigated how coloration in orange and black color morphs influences interactions with the environment by observing four behaviors—lunging, hiding, nudging, and resting—via a recorded livestream from the Monterey Bay Aquarium. Results revealed that while both morphs exhibited similar reliance on structural habitats, black clownfish displayed significantly more aggressive behaviors than orange clownfish. These findings suggest that coloration may influence social dynamics and territoriality in A. ocellaris, contributing to our understanding of how phenotypic variation shapes behavioral strategies in marine fish.
Introduction
	The Amphiprion ocellaris, a tropical marine clownfish, is found in regions ranging from Asia to Australia. This species typically displays an orange body with three white bands bordered in black along the dorsal side, though a black morph with black pigmentation instead of orange also exists, originating from captive breeding at the Vizhinjam Research Center. A. ocellaris, also known as the false clownfish, play a key role in their ecosystem by forming symbiotic relationships, particularly with anemones. The clownfish provides nutrients to the anemone, which in turn offers protection and shelter.
Anemonefish are highly territorial and form small groups consisting of a breeding pair and a few non-breeding individuals. Due to limited resources and risks associated with traveling between anemones, clownfish aggressively defend their territory rather than relocate. Both breeders and non-breeders benefit from these social groups, with selection favoring breeding pairs that tolerate non-breeders if they are distant relatives or enhance breeder size and reproductive success. Non-breeding fish may challenge breeders for dominance, with conflicts resolved non-lethally through growth regulation, as rivals attempt to outgrow each other. In stable groups, non-breeders reduce their growth to avoid conflict and eviction, while breeding pairs may suppress growth in others through harassment or food interception. 
Forming small groups lowers clownfish mortality rates compared to other reef fish, though lower-ranked individuals face higher mortality due to competition for social status and potential eviction by higher-ranked fish. Dominant clownfish regulate eviction and recruitment to prevent overpopulation at a single anemone. Gender also influences territorial defense strategies: males are more aggressive toward intruders at the periphery, while females focus on burrows guarded by males within their territory. Female territories are twice as large as male territories and depend on rank, with females always dominant over males. Male dominance is further modulated by subtle behaviors displayed by females when approaching males.
Clownfish use various signals to convey aggression or submission within their social groups. Differences in UV reflectance on anemonefish skin provide dominance and submissive cues, with fish under UV-blocking filters displaying more aggression, while those with higher UV reflectance are more likely to submit and rank lower. Amphiprion ocellaris also distinguish between species by counting the number of vertical white bars on their bodies, showing greater aggression toward their own species compared to others invading their territory. This behavior helps them identify and attack competitors using their host anemone. Additionally, clownfish use a wide range of vocalizations to structure their social hierarchy, producing aggressive sounds with threat postures and submissive sounds with head-shaking movements. These vocalizations defend territories rather than attract mates. These tactics are crucial for maintaining social balance and defending territories in anemonefish populations.
There is a gap in research comparing the behaviors of orange and black color morphs of A. ocellaris. It is unclear whether differences in coloration affect aggressive and submissive behaviors or if natural selection plays a role. Additionally, understanding these differences can reveal whether coloration influences social hierarchy within the species. The objective of this study is to examine how individual color affects specific behavioral traits within the species. This study hypothesizes that coloration influences the spatial and behavioral dynamics of A. ocellaris. Specifically, black morphs are predicted to spend more time near structures, using their darker coloration to blend into shadows and avoid predators. Identifying these behavioral differences can provide insight into whether coloration influences proximity to structures or the frequency of aggressive behaviors, such as vocalizations and posturing.
Methods
	To investigate the influence of coloration on spatial behavior in Amphiprion ocellaris, we studied both orange and black variations to assess how their colors impact their interactions with nearby structures such as coral and anemones. Observations were conducted using a 12-hour livestream from the Monterey Bay Aquarium, during which the movements and habitat use of 20 individuals of each color morph were recorded, yielding a total sample size of 40 fish.
	In this study, four distinct behavioral states of A. ocellaris clownfish were observed: lunging, hiding, nudging, and resting. Lunging was defined as a rapid, direct swimming toward another individual, indicating aggressive or territorial intent. Hiding involved urgent swimming toward a structure followed by immediate cessation of movement, with the fish positioning itself to obscure its body. Nudging was defined as gentle, purposeful physical contact with another individual, lacking any signs of aggression, such as rapid movements or flared fins. Finally, resting was defined as a state of inactivity lasting more than three seconds, not preceded by high-energy behaviors indicative of hiding.  These behaviors were selected to capture a range of aggressive, defensive, social, and inactive states.
	Total observation time and time spent near structures were recorded for each fish. Observations stopped when a fish left the field of view for more than five consecutive seconds; such intervals were subtracted from the total observation time and time near structures if applicable. Each behavior was tested for significant differences between color morphs using a non-parametric Wilcoxon rank sum test due to the non-normal distribution of data. Statistical analyses were conducted in R version 4.1.3, and figures were created using the package ‘ggplot2.’ This approach allowed for a standardized comparison of behavior and structural associations between the two color morphs. 
Results

Figure 1. Boxplot of the percentage of observed time spent near structure based on clownfish color. The median is indicated by the horizontal line in each box, IQR is indicated by the box, and outliers are shown as black points. The results of a Wilcoxon rank sum test were not significant (p = .1212). 
Regardless of color, clownfish tended to spend the majority of observation time close to structure. Median time near structure was 96.5% for black fish and 93% for orange fish; time near structure was more spread for orange fish than for black fish, indicated by interquartile ranges (IQR) of 0.165 and 0.09, respectively (Figure 1). Data for both orange and black fish were non-normally distributed, with a left skew. Results of a Wilcoxon rank sum test revealed that time spent near structure did not differ significantly between the two body colors. 
Observation of other behaviors resulted in a large number of zeroes, indicated by medians of zero for all behaviors except for instances of hiding, and only for orange fish (Figure 2c). Data for all behaviors were non-normally distributed, having a right skew. A Wilcoxon rank sum test revealed that black fish performed a significantly (p > 0.001) higher number of lunges than
orange fish (Figure 2d), while all other behaviors did not.


Figure 2. Number of specific behaviors observed based on clownfish color; (a) instances of resting, (b) instances of nudging, (c) instances of hiding, and (d) number of lunges. The median is indicated by the horizontal line in each box, IQR is indicated by the box, and outliers are shown as black points. The number of lunges differed significantly (p > 0.001) based on a Wilcoxon rank sum test, while other behaviors did not.
Discussion
	Contrary to expectations, time spent near structure did not differ significantly between clownfish color morphs. Both orange and black morphs spent the majority of their observed time near structural features, with a few outliers spending more time away. This consistent reliance on structural habitats suggests a shared ecological characteristic across both morphs. The narrower interquartile range for black morphs may indicate more uniform behavior, but coloration alone does not appear to significantly influence proximity to structures. 
These findings highlight the importance of territoriality within clownfish colonies, as individuals likely remain close to structures to avoid losing territory. The potentially lower predation risk associated with black coloration does not seem to alter this behavior, suggesting that predator avoidance plays a less significant role compared to territorial or social factors. Significant differences were observed in aggressive behaviors, with black morphs displaying more lunges than orange morphs, possibly indicating greater territorial or dominance behaviors. Other behaviors, such as resting, nudging, and hiding, showed no significant differences, except for a slightly higher frequency of hiding among orange morphs. This trend may reflect a greater reliance on defensive behaviors due to their conspicuous coloration, though the data do not strongly support this. Overall, while coloration may not significantly affect structural habitat use, it may influence social interactions and competitive dynamics within A. ocellaris populations.
The findings of this study highlight the potential influence of physical traits, such as coloration, on social and ecological interactions within fish species. While structural habitat use was consistent across color morphs of A. ocellaris, differences in aggressive behaviors suggest that physical appearance may interact with strategies like territoriality and resource defense. These results support broader ecological theories that phenotypic variation shapes individual roles in populations, influencing competition, fitness, and predator-prey dynamics. Integrating behavioral metrics with environmental context is essential for understanding how physical traits affect ecological roles. By examining these dynamics in an aquarium setting, this study provides a framework for future research linking phenotypic variation to behavioral ecology in natural environments.
Observing fish in an aquarium environment presents several limitations that  may affect the validity and generalizability of behavioral data. Controlled conditions lack the complexity of natural habitats, and structural elements may be arranged unnaturally, altering fish movement and habitat use. The absence of predators and consistent food availability reduce ecological pressures that typically shape behavior, leading to observations that may not reflect behaviors in the wild. Artificial social groupings may also affect interactions like aggression or hiding. Biases in data collection, such as the overrepresentation of conspicuous behaviors like lunging or hiding, can further skew results, while the limited field of view in a tank may prevent observation of certain behaviors. Anthropogenic factors like lighting, water flow, and the presence of cameras can also influence behavior in ways unrepresentative of natural conditions. Addressing these constraints is essential to ensure that aquarium-based studies accurately reflect the ecological and behavioral dynamics of species in their natural habitats.
The potential effects of body coloration on clownfish behavior could be further explored with larger datasets and observations under varied environmental conditions. Individual differences in aggression and territoriality may significantly influence behavior, making repeated observations of the same colony with individually tagged fish valuable for distinguishing individual traits from color morph characteristics. Observing multiple independent colonies across different aquaria would also help account for environmental variation, as specific conditions, such as higher predator presence or reduced structural cover, might reveal scenarios where coloration influences behavior. Overall, results indicate that behavioral association with habitat structure does not vary significantly between black and orange color morphs of A. ocellaris. Observation of individual behaviors suggests that black individuals displayed more aggression than orange individuals, which could be further explored in future studies.




Field Notes Report
Alex Chen
a.chen@university.edu
12/06/2024
ENV 202 Monday Section

Objectives:
	The objective of this paper is to create an overview of the overall methodology used across the tested sites and compare the differences and similarities to understand why these methods are used. The sites visited will also describe and discuss the various conditions that create the environmental structure of these data collection sites, as well as highlighting the various factors that can impact the health of fish populations. Assemblages of collected fish from the sites and jar collections will also be discussed to compare the fish species found. Understanding how these different factors can interact with one another can make it easier to reflect upon the health and stability of fish populations.
Methodology:
	At the three sites where fish collection occurred, active gear methods were deployed to catch different fish species. Active gear fishing is when the gear is moved through the water either by human force or machinery. The two ways of gear used to capture fish were pole seining and electrofishing, which both have different benefits and negatives. Electrofishing involves someone carrying an electrofishing backpack while waving a wand through the water that releases electric currents. A group of other individuals will surround the electrofisher and use hand-held nets to catch any fish immobilized by the electric currents. Electrofishing is a good method to stun fishes, but limits injury and death (Dodds & Whiles, 2020). However, the water-conductivity of a lake or river is important to consider, as low-conductivity water poorly conducts electricity and will decrease effectiveness, while high-conductivity waters will cause the electric charge to dissipate too quickly (Dodds & Whiles, 2020). Active pole seining involves two people holding the seine in the water while a group of individuals will create movement in the water while walking towards the net to guide the fish into the seine. Seine fishing can be a great method for sampling fish, such as quantifying the relative abundances of certain species (Hahn et al. 2007). However, different species can have their own selectivity or capture efficiency, which may be skewed or misrepresented if captured by pole seining (Hahn et al. 2007).
Site Descriptions:
	The Riverbend Nature Reserve (Image 1) comprises 200 acres located near the Scioto River. Located within the Scioto River floodplain, restored floodplains, vernal pools, and riparian zones can be found which creates habitats for a variety of different species. This area had rocky river bottoms, forested river sides, and shallow pools. Boggy terrains with scattered water sources could be found within the forested areas surrounding the river as well. The river had a temperature of 21.29 degrees Celsius. Water conductivity was 944 (μS/cm), dissolved oxygen was at 69.8%, and pH was recorded to be around 9.10. This area is also close to agricultural lands and urban areas, which places the water sources at risk for run-off, which can negatively impact the water quality and health of the fish. This is especially relevant as most of the lower Scioto watershed area is located in land-use areas for cultivated crops and developed land for urban and industrial areas (OEPA, 2011 ). However, despite this, the Scioto River has shown excellent macroinvertebrate health, with fish community index scores being within the excellent to good range (Table 1)(OEPA, 2011).


(Image 1): Sketch of the area where fish specimens were collected at the Riverbend Nature Reserve .
(Table 1, OEPA 2011): Table charting the overall water quality and fish community index scores of the Scioto River from 1979 to 2011.
	Cedar Creek Park (Image 2) is next to Big Walnut Creek, which is a tributary that connects the Scioto River south of the confluence between the Scioto River and Olentangy Rivers. The areas where our sampling occurred are north of the confluence between the Alum and Blacklick Creeks. The temperature of the water was 16.19 degrees Celcius, water conductivity was 476 (μS/cm), dissolved oxygen was 93.3%, and pH was 8.8. Due to Ohio’s large presence of agricultural lands, the use of fertilizer and pesticides can heavily contribute to heavy metal contamination in these watersheds (Mustafa et al. 2024). Pesticides can enter waterways and watersheds through runoff and leaching, and can negatively affect the health of fish populations and create alteration in ecosystem equilibrium (Image 3) (Mustafa et al. 2024). Big Walnut Creek also has dissolved oxygen as one of its priority causes of impairment, as habitat alterations can have negative impacts on dissolved oxygen concentrations (OEPA, 2021). To improve dissolved oxygen levels in different regions of Bug Walnut Creek, the reduction of nutrient loads and improvement of stream habitat quality are essential (OEPA, 2021).

(Image 2): Sketch of the area where fish specimens were caught at Cedar Creek Park.

(Image 3): Illustration displaying the impact heavy metal runoff and leaching can have on aquatic wildlife and human health.
The Tri-River Canoe Access (Image 4) is located at the confluence where Alum, Big Walnut, and Blacklick Creeks join together. The temperature of the water was 12.6 degrees Celsius, dissolved oxygen was 93.3%, conductivity was 669 (μS/cm), and pH was 8.05. When testing the water quality of Big Walnut Creek below the Hoover Reservoir to the Three Creeks Park confluence, the tested areas all had issues with nutrient quality and pathogens within the waterways (Table 2) (OEPA, 2021). The range between Alum Creek to Three Creeks Park confluence had issues with habitat alteration and sedimentation as well (Table 2) (OEPA, 2021). Pathogens can arise in poor-quality habitats and a lack of resistance from fish populations can cause diseases to spread that can damage the skin, gills, and digestive tracks of fish (Pękala-Safińska, 2018). Sedimentation may even impact stress response cycles within fish, which can alter developmental stages and reproductive success (Kjelland et al., 2015).

(Image 4): Sketch of the area where fish specimens were caught at Tri-River Canoe Access



(Table 2): Table of the possible health contaminants found throughout Big Walnut Creek, Alum Creek, and Blacklick Creek throughout the Three Creeks confluence.
Assemblage Comparisons:
Riverbend Nature Reserve:
	Within the Riverbend Nature Reserve by the Scioto River, many species fell under the family Leucisidae, such as the Emerald shiner (Notropis atherinoides), Suckermouth minnow (Phenacobius mirabilis), Gravel chub (Erimystax x-punctatus), and Spotfin shiner (Cyprinella spiloptera). Fish under Percidae included Banded darter (Etheostoma zonale), Rainbow darter (Etheostoma caeruleum), Slenderhead darter (Percina phoxocephala), Variegate darter (Etheostoma variatum), Greenside darter (Etheostoma blennioides), Bluebreast darter (Etheostoma camurum), Johnny darter (Etheostoma nigrum), Sand darter (Ammocrypta pellucida) and Logperch darter (Percina caprodes). Centrarchidae included Spotted black bass (Micropterus punctulatus), Longear sunfish (Lepomis megalotis), Bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus), Green sunfish (Lepomis cyanellus), Smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu), Largemouth bass (Micropterus nigricans), and Rock bass (Ambloplites rupestris). Fish in Catostomidae were Golden redhorse (Moxostoma erythrurum), Spotted sucker (Minytrema melanops), Smallmouth buffalo (Ictiobus bubalus), and Northern hogsucker (Hypentelium nigricans) were found. Brook silverside (Labidesthes sicculus) in Atherinopsidae, Blackstripe topminnow (Fundulus notatus) in Fundulidae, Yellow bullhead (Ameiurus natalis) in Ictaluridae, Longnose gar (Lepisosteus osseus) in Lepisosteidae, Western mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) in Poeciliidae, and Grass pickerel (Esox americanus) in Esocidae were also found. 
Cedar Creek Park:
	At Cedar Creek Park next to Big Walnut Creek, fish in Leucisidae included Central stoneroller minnow (Campostoma anomalum), Streamline chub (Erimystax dissimilis), Bigeye chub (Hybopsis amblops), Striped shiner (Luxilus chrysocephalus), Spotfin shiner (Cyprinella spiloptera), Bluntnose minnow (Pimephales notatus), and Silver shiner (Notropis photogenis). Percidae included Johnny darter (Etheostoma nigrum), Greenside darter (Etheostoma blennioides), Banded darter (Etheostoma zonale), Bluebreast darter (Etheostoma camurum), Fantail darter (Etheostoma flabellare), Rainbow darter (Etheostoma caeruleum), and Tippecanoe darter (Etheostoma tippecanoe). Catostomidae included Golden redhorse (Moxostoma erythrurum) and Northern hogsucker (Hypentelium nigricans). Centrarchidae included Smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu), Largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides), Longear sunfish (Lepomis megalotis), Green sunfish (Lepomis cyanellus), and Rock bass (Ambloplites rupestris). Ictaluridae had Brindled madtom (Noturus miurus), Yellow bullhead (Ameiurus natalis), and Stonecat madtom (Noturus flavus). Brook silverside (Labidesthes sicculus) in Atherinopsidae, Blackstripe topminnow (Fundulus notatus) in Fundulidae, and Western mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) in Poeciliidae were also found. 
Tri-River Canoe Access:	
Tri-River Canoe Access at the Three Creeks confluence had many fishes under Centrarchidae, with Rockbass (Ambloplites rupestris), Largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides), Spotted bass (Micropterus punctulatus), Smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu), Bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus), Green sunfish (Lepomis cyanellus), and Redear sunfish (Lepomis microlophus) were found. Under Percidae, Greenside darter (Etheostoma blennioides), Rainbow darter (Etheostoma caeruleum), Johnny darter (Etheostoma nigrum), Variegate darter (Etheostoma variatum), Banded darter (Etheostoma zonale), Tippecanoe darter (Etheostoma tippecanoe), Fantail darter (Etheostoma flabellare), and Bluebreast darter (Etheostoma camurum) were caught. Under Leucisidae, Gravel chub (Erimystax x-punctatus), Streamline chub (Erimystax dissimilis), Silver shiner (Notropis photogenis), Emerald shiner (Notropis atherinoides), Striped shiner (Luxilus chrysocephalus), Sand shiner (Notropis stramineus), Spotfin shiner (​​Cyprinella spiloptera), Suckermouth minnow (Phenacobius mirabilis), Central stoneroller minnow (Campostoma anomalum), and Bluntnose minnow (Pimephales notatus). In Catostomidae, Spotted sucker (Minytrema melanops), Northern hogsucker (Hypentelium nigricans), Golden redhorse (Moxostoma erythrurum), and Smallmouth redhorse (Moxostoma breviceps) were found. Blackstripe topminnow (Fundulus notatus) in Fundulidae and Western mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis) in Poeciliidae were also found. In Ictaluridae, Stonecat madtom (Noturus flavus) was found as well.
Environmental Differences:
	Among all of the sites, Cedar Creek Park had the highest amount of fishes under the Ictaluridae family that were captured. Fishes in Ictaluridae have evolved breathing organs to survive in harsh environments, such as low oxygen availability and high ammonia concentrations (Lisachov et al. 2023). These traits may allow various Ictaluridae species to inhabit locations such as Cedar Creek Park due to their evolved ability to adapt to the varying dissolved oxygen percentages. Ictaluridae species have also been noted to be able to have higher tolerances to organophosphorous insecticides, and have been recorded as being less susceptible to the effects of pesticides and insecticides compared to other species (Macek & Mcallister, 1970). 
Riverbend Nature Reserve had the highest diversity of Percidae. Darter species are adapted to live in fast-moving sections of rocky streams and rivers, and to prevent being pushed downstream many species have developed reduced swim bladders or have no swim bladders (MDC). Flow speed of the water can also impact swim bladder size, and swim bladder volume was found to be smaller in locations where fast currents occurred (Evans & Page, 2002). Riverbend Nature Reserve had a rocky stream bottom with a strong current, which would suit the conditions that darters inhabit. 
Cedar Creek Park had the least amount of species while Three Creeks had the most. Tri-River Canoe Access is located near the Three Creeks confluence, and river confluences are unique hydrological processes that result in a complex flow structure and water quality mixing (Yuan et al., 2023). In these areas, there is great food availability and habitat complexity that can host increased diversity and productivity of fish (Yuan et al., 2023). Confluences have been shown to have high spatial heterogeneity of fish size, density, and species (Yuan et al., 2023). Three Creeks include the confluence of Alum, Big Walnut, and Blacklick Creeks, which opens up more diverse habitats for a variety of fish species.
Grass pickerel were only found in the Riverbend Nature Reserve. Grass pickerel can be found in habitats that are shallow, slow-moving, and heavily vegetated (FOC). Their habitats normally include aquatic vegetation, logs, and woody structures (FOC). They are classified as a warmwater species and usually prefer temperatures around 26 degrees Celcius (FOC). While the main portion of the Scioto River stream where many of our darter species came from, the sides of the stream had many shallow, slow-moving, or stagnant waters that were heavily vegetated. Due to the proximity of the forest to this stream, there was an abundance of woody structures and logs which also provide ample habitat and protection to Grass pickerel. 
Conclusion:
	Throughout Ohio, there are a variety of different habitat and ecosystem structures that are home to a diverse array of fish species. To collect data on diversity, multiple methods should be utilized to have an unbiased collection of specimens to understand the distribution of species. Throughout the different sites tested, a variety of habitat conditions were seen, which contributed to the differences in fish species found. Understanding the different dynamics of these sites can help researchers understand which variables may impact different species and can be used for management to protect and conserve specific species.







Point Sampling in Hardwood Forests at Camp Forest Hills, Springfield IL

By

Alex Chen

Presented to Prof. Jamie Smith

In Partial Fulfillment of the Requirements for
ENV 101
04/21/2025






Introduction
Ensuring accurate forest inventory is essential for creating sustainable forest management. Point sampling, or variable radius plot sampling, is often used to help estimate per-acre and tract values for basal area, tree density, and timber volume, to better understand current and future resources (Lund, 1982). This method employs a Basal Area Factor (BAF) prism in or to select trees that are proportional to their cross-sectional area (Lund, 1982). In point sampling, sample points are used as reference centers for collecting measurements of surrounding trees. These points do not represent the physical area, but instead acts as an anchor for the sampling process by determining which trees are included in a plot based on limiting distances using a prism (Lund, 1982). The use of a BAF prism allows for the inclusion of trees in proportion to the basal area, which can be an efficient method in uneven-aged stands (Lund, 1982). The point sampling method is an important resource for inventory frameworks and can help track possible temporal and spatial changes in forest conditions, and facilitates faster data collection over larger areas (Lund, 1982).
The survey conducted at Camp Forest Hills, Springfield Illinois, used a BAF 10 prism and included all trees above five inch diameter at breast height (DBH). Merchantable volume was recorded for pulpwood (8’ sticks to 4” top diameter) and sawlogs (10” minimum top diameter, measured in ½-log increments). With the data collected from this survey, the results will be compared to a previous survey using the fixed area plot cruise method, using CV%. Strip cruise, fixed area plot, and point sampling will be compared and an analysis of the pros and cons of using individual tally sheets or cumulative tally sheets will be included as well.


Methods
In a field crew of 4, at Camp Forest Hills in Springfield, IL on April 8, 2025, a forest stand was evaluated using the point sampling techniques. The latitude and longitude were 41°50'00"N 87°39'00"W, and the forest stand was mostly comprised of hardwood species such as oaks, maples, and hickories. The equipment comprised of a map of the site, 15 tally sheets, two cruising/Biltmore sticks, two compasses, two logger’s tape, a clipboard, and a Suunto Clinometer.
Plots were established based on the provided map (Figure 1), with a plot point established every 3 chains. 7 plots in total were established and tallied for (Figure 2) At each plot, a BAF 10 prism was used to determine which trees were “in” or “out” of the plot and if they needed to be measured. Trees that were “in” were measured using either a Biltmore stick or logger’s tape. All trees within the plot were measured at DBH using 2” scale D-classes, and trees that were in the 6-inch to 10-inch class or larger trees with a lack of adequate sawlog were evaluated as pulpwood. Trees in the 12-inch class and above were measured as sawlog values to the nearest  ½ log. Each tree was only tallied once. Trees that were considered borderline had their distance from the tree center to the plot center measured, and if it was smaller than the R value found in piR^2, then the tree was considered in.The dot-tally method was used to record the trees in each plot, with one tally sheet per plot. This data was then used to create a stand and stock table (Table 1), with attached equations explaining how these values were calculated (Appendix D).



Discussion
	Within the per-acre estimates, there was a notable concentration of pulpwood and cords within the 14-22 inch classes. Pulpwood had its highest values in the 8 inch class, and sawlog values had its highest values in the class as well. The variability across the DBH class is indicated by their high standard deviations and wide confidence intervals. This variability is common in uneven-aged stands, or in forests going through a transition period due to natural disturbances or management. There was a low amount of trees found in ≥32" DBH classes, which may indicate that these trees may not have had enough time to grow into the upper classes, possibly due to insufficient time since stand initiation. 
	When comparing the coefficient of variation between point sampling and fixed area plot sampling, both had large CV% for pulpwood values per entire tract, with point sampling with a CV% of 155.6% and fixed area plot CV% of 156.07%. These high CV% in both sampling methods indicate variability in the pulpwood volume values between the diameter classes and tally point cheers. This is usually expected in point sampling, since larger trees have a greater influence on estimates since they are more likely to be included within a plot due to being tied to their basal area. Both methods also had high sawlog CV% values as well. This variability is common in point sampling when less larger trees are measured during sampling, and also reflects the sensitivity of using point sampling to measure larger trees with more merchantable volume.
	Point sampling can be beneficial when measuring stands where larger trees make up a large portion of the stand values. However it can also introduce higher variability in uneven-aged stands. Fixed area plots may offer more consistent estimates in more uniform stands, but can sometimes under-represent larger trees unless the plot size is adjusted. Strip cruising can provide clear spatial coverage and is effective at mapping stand variation, but is not as efficient in obstructed terrain and may have biases depending on where the strips are placed. Fixed area plots are useful for stands with more uniform spacing and are compatible with a wide range of forest attributes, but may underrepresent certain trees and there is fixed effort per plot. Point sampling is efficient for sampling basal area and volume, and fewer plots are required, but can be biased in stands with variable size classes and towards larger trees.

Tally sheets are another factor to consider when doing surveys. Individual tally sheets are beneficial for statistical analysis for mean per plot and standard deviation and makes error checking easier to decipher, but requires more data management and can sometimes lead to transcription errors. Cumulative tally sheets can streamline data collection and reduce the risk of plot mislabeling, but can make it difficult to calculate CV% and confidence intervals and loses variance estimation.

Conclusion
	Point sampling can be an effective method for collecting data such as basal area, tree density, and timber volume, and can be less labor intensive and have faster data collection in comparison to methods such as strip cruises and fixed area plots. Point sampling can be effective for uneven-aged stands, but does come with the bias of over-representing larger trees due to their tendency to be included in the view of the BAF prism. When choosing a method to use in the field, it is important to observe the site and the time limit you have to complete a survey. It is also important to consider how you will record your data, as cumulative tally sheets and individual sheets come with positives and negatives depending on what you want to accomplish in the field or when analyzing data afterwards. 

Task:
 Can you analyze my past field reports and help identify my most consistent blind spot or weakness when it comes to addressing experimental limitations and environmental variables. Based on these 4 reports, also generate a highly targeted piece of reflective advice on how I can redesign my future methodologies to account for this overarching flaw.

After reviewing your four field reports, a consistent blind spot emerges in your approach to experimental design: a tendency towards **methodological complacency**. You demonstrate a strong ability to *identify* limitations and environmental variables, but your methodology often proceeds with known flaws, addressing these issues retrospectively in the discussion rather than proactively designing them out of the experiment.

Your work consistently follows a pattern:
1.  You choose a methodology (point sampling, aquarium observation, observational fish survey).
2.  You acknowledge in the discussion that this method has known weaknesses for the given context (e.g., point sampling's bias towards large trees in an uneven-aged stand; an aquarium's artificiality for studying natural fish behavior; an observational survey's inability to prove causation).
3.  You then present the results generated by this compromised design.
4.  Finally, you list the limitations again, suggesting they be considered in future work.

While self-critique is a valuable skill, the weakness lies in not integrating the solutions to these known problems into the initial design phase. You are reacting to limitations instead of preempting them.

### Reflective Advice: From Reactive Critique to Proactive Design

To elevate your research, you must shift from a mindset of "What were the limitations of this study?" to "How will I design a study that minimizes these limitations from the start?" This requires a "pre-mortem" analysis before you ever step into the field or begin observations.

Here is a targeted, four-step strategy to redesign your future methodologies:

**Step 1: Conduct a Pre-Mortem Analysis**
Before your next project, write a "Methodological Limitations & Mitigation Plan." For your proposed design, brainstorm every potential source of bias, noise, or confounding variable. For each one, you must define a specific mitigation strategy. Do not proceed until you have a plan for the most critical ones.

**Step 2: Redesign Your Methodologies Based on Past Flaws**
Apply this principle directly to the weaknesses seen in your past reports:

*   **Flaw Seen in Clownfish Study (Report 2): Using an Artificial Environment.**
    *   **Past Approach:** You used a single aquarium livestream, knowing it lacked predators, natural grouping, and complexity. You then discussed these limitations in the discussion.
    *   **Proactive Redesign:** Reframe the objective. If you wish to study natural behavior, you cannot use an aquarium. A redesigned study would either:
        *   **(Ideal)** Transition to a field observation study at a reef, or a mesocosm experiment where you build multiple, replicated tanks mimicking natural conditions (with predators, varied structures, and naturalistic social groupings).
        *   **(If constrained)** Clearly state that the study's conclusion is restricted *only* to aquarium-reared *A. ocellaris* and cannot be generalized to wild populations. The methodology would be designed to answer a question about captive behavior, not natural behavior.

*   **Flaw Seen in Forest Inventory (Report 1): Using a Biased Method in a Known Context.**
    *   **Past Approach:** You used a BAF 10 prism in an uneven-aged stand, noted the resulting high variability (CV% > 150%), and attributed it to the method's bias towards large trees.
    *   **Proactive Redesign:** Anticipate the bias. If working in an uneven-aged stand is unavoidable, your design should account for it. Options include:
        *   Using a lower BAF (e.g., BAF 5) to increase the probability of including smaller trees.
        *   Implementing a stratified sampling design, using point sampling in dense areas and fixed-area plots in open areas.
        *   Combining methods: use point sampling for a quick basal area estimate, and supplement it with fixed-area plots in representative locations to get more reliable volume and density data for specific size classes.

*   **Flaw Seen in Fish Survey (Report 3): Correlational Observation Without Controlling Variables.**
    *   **Past Approach:** You brilliantly described the environmental variables (conductivity, DO, etc.) and linked them to species presence, but your analysis remained qualitative. You observed correlations without testing them.
    *   **Proactive Redesign:** Integrate environmental variables as predictors in your analysis. Instead of just listing species per site, design a quantitative analysis (like a canonical correspondence analysis or a multivariate regression) to statistically model how water quality parameters (your independent variables) explain the variation in fish assemblage composition (your dependent variable). This turns your descriptive observations into a predictive framework.

**Step 3: Distinguish Between Description and Causal Inference**
Be explicit about what your study can and cannot claim. Your fish survey (Report 3) was an excellent *description* of site differences. Frame it as such. Avoid implying causation (e.g., "sedimentation *impacted* stress") when you only have correlation. A proactive design would seek to establish causation through controlled experiments or robust statistical controls.

**Step 4: Document the Mitigation, Not Just the Problem**
In your final report, don't just have a "Limitations" section. Add a "Methodological Rigor" or "Mitigation of Bias" section. Here, you can state: "We recognized that [known flaw] could bias results. To mitigate this, we [describe the proactive step you took, e.g., 'used a BAF 5 prism,' 'sampled along a pollution gradient,' 'controlled for tank effects by...']."

By adopting this proactive, design-first approach, you will transform your research from a series of interesting but methodologically compromised case studies into a robust body of work whose conclusions are well-supported by a sound experimental framework. You move from being a critic of your own work to an architect of its integrity.
